This dynamic nature creates a tension between latency (the time it takes to generate the first token and subsequent tokens) and throughput (the number of tokens or requests processed per second). An LLM processes an input sequence of tokens through multiple layers of attention and feed-forward networks. # Advanced LLM Inference Optimization: A Technical Deep Dive

Large Language Models (LLMs) have transitioned from research curiosities to critical infrastructure components in modern software stacks. However, serving these models in production environments presents unique challenges distinct from traditional machine learning inference. Unlike classification models that process fixed-size inputs and produce fixed-size outputs, LLMs are autoregressive generators. They produce text token-by-token, where each new token depends on the entire history of previously generated tokens. This sequential dependency creates a fundamental bottleneck in throughput and latency.

To address these challenges, modern inference servers (such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and Hugging Face TGI) have developed sophisticated optimization techniques. This tutorial explores the core mechanisms that enable high-performance LLM serving: Continuous Batching, Key-Value (KV) Caches, Prefix Reuse, and Speculative Decoding. We will also analyze the critical trade-offs between latency and throughput that engineers must navigate.

## 1. The Fundamental Bottleneck: Autoregressive Generation

To understand why optimization is necessary, we must first understand the computational graph of an LLM. During the **prefill phase**, the model processes the entire input prompt in parallel. This is computationally intensive but highly parallelizable, making it efficient on GPUs. During the **decode phase**, the model generates one token at a time. For each step, the model must attend to all previous tokens (the context) to predict the next one.

If we were to serve requests naively, we would process one request at a time. This leads to severe GPU underutilization because the memory bandwidth required to load model weights for a single token generation is high, but the compute utilization is low. Furthermore, if we use static batching (grouping requests of similar length), we encounter the "straggler problem." If a batch contains one request that needs to generate 500 tokens and another that needs only 10, the entire batch must wait for the 500-token request to finish before the GPU can start processing the next batch. The GPU sits idle for the majority of the time waiting for the long request to complete, while the short request has already finished.
